# Practical AI use {#sec-practical-ai-use}

You now know what the assistant is doing under the hood, and you have practised predicting, explaining, and confirming with it a few times. This note is smaller than those and more useful in the moment. It collects some ordinary habits for actually typing at the thing, so that the answers you get back are worth the checking you are about to give them. None of it is about which button to click. Buttons change every few months, and the habits below do not.

It is worth saying what this note is not. It is not a list of magic phrases that make the assistant more reliable. There is no such phrase, and a machine that produces plausible continuations will keep producing plausible continuations however politely you ask. What good habits buy you is something more modest and more useful, which is answers that are specific enough to be checked, and enough clarity about what you asked for that you can tell when you did not get it.

## Say what you want, not what you are thinking about {#sec-be-specific}

Something about DNA sequences is not a request, it is a mood. A function that takes a DNA string and returns the count of each base as a dictionary is a request. The difference matters more than it would with a person, because the assistant fills the gaps you leave with a plausible guess rather than with a clarifying question. A vague prompt does not get you a cautious answer. It gets you a confident answer to a question you did not quite ask, and the confidence is identical either way.

The fix costs you nothing but a few extra words. Name the input, name the output, and if there is an edge case you already care about, such as lowercase letters or an empty string or a sequence whose length is not a multiple of three, say so up front. Naming the edge case does two things at once. It makes the answer more likely to handle the case, and, more importantly, it means you have already decided what correct behaviour would be, which is exactly what you will need in order to check the answer.

There is a hidden benefit here that is easy to miss. Writing a precise request forces you to work out what you actually want, and quite often that is the hard part of the problem. Students regularly discover, halfway through typing a careful prompt, that they now know how to write the function themselves. That is not wasted effort. That is the effort.

## Give it the context it actually needs, and no more {#sec-context}

If you want help with one function inside a larger project, paste that function and the one or two things it depends on, not the whole file. Too little context and the assistant guesses at conventions you already decided. Too much and it starts guessing at which of forty things you actually meant, which is its own kind of vagueness. A good rule of thumb is to give it what a classmate would need in order to help you, no more and no less.

Include the real error message when there is one, in full, rather than your summary of it. A traceback is precise, and your paraphrase of it is a claim about what went wrong that may already be the mistake. Include the actual input you ran it on, too, if the failure depends on the data. What you should not include is your theory about the cause, at least not first, because stating your theory is the most reliable way to be told your theory is correct.

## Read the reply before you trust the tone {#sec-tone}

A reply is fluent and confident whether it is right or wrong, so confidence is not evidence of anything, and you should stop letting it feel like evidence. This is harder than it sounds, because the reading habits you have built over a lifetime treat fluency as a rough signal of competence, and for human writers that signal is not completely useless. Here it carries no information at all. The same process produced the confident correct answer and the confident wrong one.

Read a reply the way you would read a claim from a classmate who is occasionally brilliant and occasionally makes things up with total sincerity. Interesting, worth considering, and not yet worth acting on.

## Ask for the reasoning, but do not mistake it for proof {#sec-reasoning}

You can ask the assistant to explain a line, walk through an example, or justify a choice, and doing so often surfaces a mistake that a bare answer would have hidden. It is a genuinely good habit and you should keep it. But remember what an explanation is. It is another plausible-sounding piece of text, generated the same way the original answer was, and generated after the answer rather than before it. It is not a report of how the answer was reached, because there is no such report to give.

This means an explanation can make a wrong answer sound more convincing exactly as easily as it can reveal that the answer was wrong. Treat an explanation as a second thing to check, never as the checking itself.

## Tell helpful apart from merely fluent {#sec-helpful-vs-fluent}

A helpful answer is one you can act on because you have verified it, by running it, testing it, or checking it against something you already know. A merely fluent answer is one that reads well and that you have not yet checked. The two are indistinguishable by feel, which is the entire point of this course, and they are distinguishable only by the running, testing, or checking you actually do.

If you take one habit from this note, take this one. Before you accept an answer, ask yourself what you would have to see in order to know it was wrong. If you cannot name anything, you have not been given a checkable claim, and the next thing to do is to ask again more precisely rather than to proceed.

#### Exercise {#sec-ex-two-prompts}

`AI: Explainer`

Ask the assistant the same underspecified question two different ways. First ask something genuinely vague, such as writing you something to look at a DNA sequence, and then ask a precise request naming the input, the output, and one edge case you care about. Compare the two replies. Which one would you have had to guess at, and which one can you actually check against what you asked for?

#### Exercise {#sec-ex-falsify}

`SOLO`

Take the precise reply from the previous exercise and, without running anything and without asking anything further, write down one concrete input for which you could tell whether the code is right, together with the output you would expect. If you cannot produce such an input, that tells you the request was still not precise enough, and it is worth working out which part of it was the vague part.

For your logbook this week, write down the single worst prompt you have given the assistant so far in this course, from memory or from your prompt history, and rewrite it as it should have been. Say what the rewrite would have let you check that the original did not.
